narrative: During the 2000s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture experienced a resurgence of interest in natural textures and traditional styles. The afro, a hairstyle created by combing out natural growth or styling with chemical curling products, became increasingly popular as part of the natural hair movement. Cornrows, a traditional African braiding practice, were also widely adopted, often styled in simple lines or elaborate designs. Dreadlocks, which can form naturally or be created through techniques like twisting and backcombing, gained popularity among some individuals. Protective hairstyles, such as box braids and Bantu knots, remained popular for their ability to minimize hair breakage and environmental damage. While the source material does not provide extensive documentation on this era, it suggests that there was a growing emphasis on embracing natural textures and traditional styles as part of Black and African identity.
